data.title: Canada rejects US terms for trade deal as 50 percent tariffs take effect
data.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pulled his country’s negotiators from trade talks with the U.S. on Friday evening, just hours before the Trump administration’s new round of tariffs were set to go into effect. 

This decision followed weeks of intense negotiations between the two nations over President Trump’s proposed 50 percent tariffs on over $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. 

These new tariffs — which were originally scheduled to go into effect on Wednesday — would impact a range of goods, including wine, hockey sticks, cement, plywood and more. The prime minister has said these new policies are in “direct violation” of the free trade agreement between the U.S., Mexico and Canada. 

Carney vowed to “match those tariffs dollar for dollar” in a statement released Friday evening on social media. He added that Canada’s government will present “additional measures” to support workers and business owners in the country in the coming days. 

While the prime minister noted Canadian negotiators made “significant progress” in recent weeks, he said this had “not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”

“As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa,” he said in his statement.

“They have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute,” Carney continued. “However, last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer slammed Canada over its decision to walk away from these discussions in a statement shared on his official social media page.

“Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” Greer wrote, calling this a “missed opportunity” for a partnership between the two nations.

Canada and the U.S. have historically enjoyed a close relationship, but the Trump administration’s aggressive efforts to broker new trade agreements that favor the U.S. have placed these ties to the test. 

Trump has repeatedly suggested that the U.S. cede its northern neighbor as a “51st state” and addressed Carney as the “future governor of Canada.”

Carney wrote that Canada’s negotiators in these tariff discussions have “worked in that context.”

“We have recognized from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship,” Carney continued. “Our government understood, before many, that America is altering all its trade relationships. Putting tariffs on its closest allies and charging access for its vast market.”

data.title: 'Shocking' fake poll firm puts industry under the microscope: 'Unfortunately not surprising'
data.description:
The revelation that two polls released in recent weeks from a purported polling firm were faked is adding a new curveball for a polling industry already trying to improve public trust in its work. 

Median Strategies made the stunning announcement earlier this past week that its poll results of the Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary and the Los Angeles mayoral race were not real and instead were put out as part of a “social experiment.” It said they should not be cited or treated as legitimate data.

Coming off well-publicized polling misses in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary and the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, the timing of the ploy wasn’t helpful either. 

Pollsters said this incident emphasizes the due diligence that media outlets and the public must conduct when looking at and trying to understand numbers being released. 

“It was very shocking, but unfortunately not surprising,” Ben Leff, the CEO of the polling and survey research firm Verasight, said about Median’s fake polls. “I think the industry and media are used to probably polls that aren’t conducted very well in terms of rigorous methods or how they’re verifying respondents, but this was sort of the extreme of that, where everything was completely fake.” 

The polling industry has already been dealing for years with struggles to improve its credibility in the eyes of the public, with trust shaken by President Trump’s repeated outperformances in 2016, 2020 and 2024, to varying extents. 

But that has been at least based on good-faith efforts from pollsters trying to model what an election may look like the best they can. That’s a different situation from Median, which pollsters emphasized shouldn’t be considered part of the industry. 

Median first released a poll on the Los Angeles mayor’s race, a contest that hasn’t seen any major public polling conducted since the primary election in June. It showed Mayor Karen Bass (D) leading progressive City Council member Nithya Raman (D) by 12 points, a lead that Bass touted in a later-deleted post on the social platform X. 

After Median revealed the poll was fake, Bass’s campaign denounced it, with a spokesperson calling for any “bad faith attempts to influence elections” to be “investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” 

Raman’s campaign attacked Bass for promoting a “fake poll without properly vetting the source.” 

A second fake poll from Median showed Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong leading the state’s Democratic primary for governor by 20 points. The democratic socialist ultimately lost the primary earlier this month in a major upset. 

The poll’s result was largely in line with what several other polls from legitimate firms were indicating, though polling was limited in the primary race’s final weeks. 

The extent to which the poll influenced expectations, and potentially turnout in the race, is impossible to quantify, but the more immediate impact may be how polls are perceived as the country is gearing up for the critical midterm elections in November. 

Geoffrey Skelley, the chief elections analyst at Decision Desk HQ, noted the impact is different than if a major pollster was revealed to be falsifying data. But he said he understands how this could affect perception. 

“I understand why, say in the aftermath of 2016, people have that attitude,” he said. “That is concerning, that it sort of adds fuel to the fire of ‘The polls are worthless,’ ‘The polls are meaningless,’ ‘They’re not even real’-kind of conversation.” 

Median maintained on its website that it wanted to see what would happen if it put out fake polls. 

“Median Strategies was created as a short-term social experiment examining how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification,” its message read. 

Median did not return a request from The Hill for comment. 

The Guardian identified the source behind Median as 21-year-old Rahil Prakash, a recent college graduate. He said he was inspired by the polling miss in the Michigan Senate primary to see if fake polls could “penetrate the ecosystem” easily.

“I was a bit shocked, perhaps at how fast this sort of information can spread,” he said.

Prakash said he wanted to apologize to the Bass, Raman and Hong campaigns.

“And I hope it gives a really good lesson going forward in that we need to be very serious about these things and very serious in how, if one person can do this, what can a serious operation do in the future,” he said.

Experts expressed skepticism about Median’s claims about its motive, noting various political or financial incentives for the results. The rise of prediction markets in recent years gives another potential impact on this, as bettors place wagers on a wide range of questions, including on who will win an election. Prakash told The Guardian he placed no bets on the races.

Skelley said fake pollsters have put out results in the past intended to influence prediction markets and make money off the impacts. But they have generally not come off looking as legitimate as Median did, either not having a website or having a suspicious-looking one. 

Leff said the first step that media outlets and members of the public should do if they see a poll from a pollster they don’t recognize is check if the pollster is a member of the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative. 

He said the initiative is similar to the bar for attorneys and provides credentials to pollsters that are transparent about disclosing their methodologies in detail. 

He said a second step is looking for a detailed methodology statement provided to the public included in the poll’s release. That statement would include information such as the number of respondents, margin of error and how respondents were recruited. 

Leff said Median had a “top-line” report of its methodology that didn’t provide a lot of details. 

“That was immediately a red flag to us,” he said. 

Of course, even a detailed methodology statement could still be faked, and conducting a deep dive may be more extensive than the average person knows to do or takes the time for. 

John Cluverius, the director of survey research for the UMass Lowell Center for Public Opinion, said this underscores the importance of not giving too much emphasis to any single poll but what pictures various polls from different pollsters are painting. 

“Thinking about polls in terms of them being different snapshots that are trying to measure the same thing, I think that’s very useful,” he said. 

Cluverius said he believes media outlets have become “smarter” about insisting on transparency from polling firms, becoming more selective in which polls they cover and don’t, which can help weed out those that are faulty. 

Leff noted this is just one of the threats the polling industry faces, pointing to bots and artificial intelligence that attempt to take surveys. 

In another incident, the polling aggregator FiftyPlusOne announced Thursday that it would “permanently ban” one polling firm and suspend another over a lack of disclosure that Florida GOP gubernatorial candidate James Fishback’s campaign was funding them. The banned firm was also accused of fabricating data, a claim that it denies. 

Ryan O’Donnell, the executive director of the left-leaning pollster Data for Progress, said the takeaway from the controversy needs to be more vigilance. 

“The lesson here isn’t that we should stop trusting polling — understanding public opinion is vital to a functioning democracy and there are plenty of credible, trustworthy pollsters out there,” he said. “People just need to know what to look for.”

Sarah Fortinsky contributed.

data.title: 5 things to know about the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington
data.description:
The streets of Washington will be filled with the roars of professional motor sports this weekend as the IndyCar Series brings its high-speed show to the nation’s capital for the first time ever during the final stretch of its 2026 season. 

The event, which spans two days and will close streets around the National Mall and downtown D.C., is being billed as one of the final spectacles commemorating the country’s 250th birthday at the behest of President Trump.  

Here’s everything you need to know ahead of Sunday’s Grand Prix in D.C. 

Race is punctuation mark on Freedom 250  

Sunday’s race will mark a dramatic conclusion to a summer in D.C. that came with a slew of major sports and cultural events presided over by Trump’s administration.  

The president hosted the Great American State Fair, facilitated a UFC primetime fight just outside the White House and delivered an address to the nation on July 4 before one of the largest fireworks displays downtown D.C. has seen.   

This weekend’s race was not on the initial 2026 IndyCar schedule, and it came at Trump’s behest.

Trump reportedly had been musing about a road race on D.C. streets for months, and in January, he directed the departments of Transportation and the Interior to designate a race route through the National Mall.  

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix will serve as the first auto race held on the streets of the nation’s capital, with organizers saying this week it will likely be a “one-and-done” event.  

Top Trump administration officials, like Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, are seeking to cast the event as a moment of unity for the country.  

“And I think if you look at the political divide in America, this is an event that brings America together,” Duffy told the New York Post this week. “Cars and racing is freedom and American.” 

Trump and first lady Melania Trump are expected to take a ceremonial lap around the course in “The Beast” on Sunday before the race starts, likely drawing even more attention to the unique end-of-summer showcase.  

IndyCar looking to create the right ‘visuals’  

The race for the IndyCar championship is entering its final stretch, and several of the sport’s top names will be racing this weekend in D.C.  

Series points leader Álex Palou will be in the field, along with top-ranked American Kyle Kirkwood, both of whom feature cars built by Honda Racing.   

The action starts Saturday with two practice races. Qualifying is set for that afternoon.  

Sunday’s race day activities will begin with a warmup at 9 a.m. before President Trump waves the green flag at 1 p.m.  

Those who follow the sport closely say Sunday’s spectacle will be a major moment for a racing league that has catered largely to a niche audience for decades.  

“It’s all about the visual for me. You know, time and place,” longtime motor sports journalist Curt Cavin wrote this week. “The visuals of the U.S. Capitol, Washington Monument, White House and the rest of the elements that make the city the most recognizable in the world will give the sport much-craved relevance. Everything else is secondary, including the actual race, which at close to three hours will be interesting in itself. Let’s see how cool all of this looks.”  

Race day will have a major impact on life in D.C. 

The buildout for Sunday’s race has been underway for weeks, closing city streets and making things difficult for commuters during a usually sleepy time of year in the district, when schools are closed and Congress is on recess.   

In addition to the 1.7-mile track featuring seven turns or 147 laps, IndyCar has put up massive hospitality suites, fenced off sidewalks on major downtown thoroughfares and left much of the usually busy National Mall unpassable to vehicle or pedestrian traffic during the tourist season.   

Local officials have been urging D.C. residents who do not plan to attend the race to stay away from the area all weekend, while those who do have tickets should seek public transportation to get to their designated viewing areas.   

“This is worse than cherry blossom,” D.C. commuter Nancy Marlow told local radio station WTOP this week, referencing the annual springtime festival that draws thousands to D.C.’s Tidal Basin. “I’ve been out here over an hour. This time of year, it normally takes me 20 minutes.” 

Other spots further from the racetrack have also been impacted, like the small streets near the Lincoln Memorial, which was closed briefly Friday while a promo for the race’s television coverage was being filmed.  

Critics raise noise concerns 

Anyone who has ever been to an IndyCar race knows the races are, if nothing else, loud and can cause the ground to shake.  

This has been a major point of concern for D.C. residents, business owners and operators of iconic district museums and art galleries that are either directly along the racetrack or not far away.  

In a letter sent to the National Park Service late last month, the nonprofit New Living Deal raised concern the race “may harm historic properties directly adjacent to the race course.”  

“Such vibrations are well above normal street traffic and even go beyond those of jackhammers, pile drivers, and even freight trains, which are commonly mitigated pieces of equipment during construction projects for noise as well as vibration due to their extremely high potential for impacts,” the nonprofit wrote. “Like many others across the nation, we question the necessity and cost of this event and seek clarity about the steps we assume are already being taken to mitigate adverse effects and harm to historic structures surrounding the proposed race course.”  

A spokesperson for the National Gallery of Art told WTOP it had conducted a vibration study in preparation for the race and put forth “a set of measures to ensure the safety of our staff, visitors, collection and facilities.” 

Race will pass key D.C. landmarks 

Spanning 1.7 miles, Sunday’s race will wind through some of D.C.’s most notable downtown streets and pass dozens of iconic landmarks and federal buildings. 

The start and finish line has been placed on 3rd Street NW between Pennsylvania and Maryland avenues, just blocks from the U.S. Capitol.  

Racers’ first turn will be west on Pennsylvania Avenue, where they will speed past the National Gallery of Art and National Archives before heading south on 9th Street NW past the Smithsonian.

The race track turns again on 7th Street NW through the heart of the National Mall, where the White House and Capitol will be most visible from inside a racer’s vehicle.  

The final stretch of the race will come along Independence Avenue SW, where drivers will head east before a sharp left turn at the National Museum of the American Indian and up 3rd Street NW toward the finish line and Delta 250 suites full of VIPs set to include President Trump.

data.title: Trump administration wants to deny ABA ability to oversee law schools: Report
data.description:
The Department of Education has suggested ending the American Bar Association’s (ABA) oversight on the law school accreditation process.

The ABA has had the power to accredit nearly 200 law schools over the last 70 years, but this power may come to an end, according to a Wall Street Journal report. The department made its first official move to limit the association’s power on Friday.

Assistant Education Secretary David Barker told the Journal that he sees the accreditation process “like a cartel,” as many of these oversight agencies lack competition. He added that the model allows accreditors to “feel free to inject their own political preferences.”

Chair of the ABA’s Accreditation Council Melissa Hart wrote in a statement to the Journal that the Education Department’s move was “one step in the regular recognition process that the Council and other accreditors periodically complete.”

“A hearing is the next step in that process, and we’re confident the Council will address any concerns the Department may have at that hearing,” she added.

The accreditation process acts as an educational quality check that also determines whether students at a given higher education institution will have access to federal loans. In many states, a law student who did not attend an ABA-accredited program cannot take the bar exam.

The ABA and Department of Education did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

This attack to the ABA’s power falls within a broader pattern within the Trump administration, as officials continue to leverage grants and government funding to keep educational institutions on a short leash. 

In March, for example, The Department of Education announced it would investigate more than 50 colleges and universities over alleged “racial preferences” in admissions and academics.

The ABA similarly faced pressure in May to roll back Standard 206, which stated law schools desiring accreditation must “demonstrate by concrete action a commitment to diversity and inclusion.”

Republicans have also accused the association of harboring left-leaning political biases. In late 2025, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier (R) referred to the ABA as an arm of a political left-wing party.”

In February 2025, Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson barred political appointees from renewing their ABA membership, writing in a letter to staff that the association “advances radical left-wing causes and promotes the business interests of Big Tech.”

data.title: Leavitt to work at Trump-affiliated super PAC following White House departure
data.description:
Karoline Leavitt is set to work at President’s Trump MAGA Inc. super PAC following her departure from the White House, the outgoing press secretary confirmed Friday.

Leavitt shared her next career move with reporters outside of Air Force One Friday evening, a little over one week after she announced she would step down at the end of August to spend more time with her family.

She did not elaborate on what her title would be a MAGA Inc. — a Trump and GOP-aligned PAC reportedly sitting on over $350 million in campaign funds ahead of November’s midterms. Leavitt served as a spokesperson for the PAC before joining the president’s 2024 campaign.

“You guys will still see me all the time,” the outgoing press secretary told reporters Friday.

Leavitt also added that the Friday evening flight — a trip to Myrtle Beach, S.C. for a Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) rally featuring the president — would be her last official outing as press secretary.

After Leavitt announced her departure, Trump said she would continue working with the White House as one of his “top advisers” and be an “influential voice within the Republican Party.” The press secretary herself said in her announcement that her “fight” against the Democratic Party would not end once she vacated the post.

The White House notably did not name an immediate replacement for Leavitt, who had returned from maternity leave in mid-July shortly before deciding to permanently leave the role. Trump commented on mounting speculation surrounding who would be her replacement, signaling that he had several options and that the choice would be difficult.

“I will tell you this, and Karoline will tell you this, I have never seen so many job applications in my life,” Trump told reporters Friday.

Top contenders for the role reportedly include CNN conservative commentator Scott Jennings and Katie Miller, the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, among others.

Although Leavitt confirmed the Myrtle Beach rally would be her last event serving as press secretary, she said Friday that she still planned to join the president throughout the midterms campaign trail, including at September’s GOP convention in Dallas.

data.title: Army Secretary eyes exit around end of year amid Hegseth tensions
data.description:
Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is looking to leave his role at the Pentagon around the end of 2026 following a months-long turf war with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a former White House official and another source familiar with the discussions told The Hill on Friday. 

A third source familiar said Driscoll has long communicated that between 23 and 24 months is the lifetime of an Army secretary in the Trump administration. Driscoll, an ally of Vice President Vance, was confirmed by the Senate on Feb. 25 last year in a 66-28 vote. 

Driscoll’s spokesperson declined to comment. 

The Army Secretary has pushed the service branch to improve living conditions for service members, modernize equipment and learn from Ukrainian forces how to utilize commercial technology in modern warfare. 

One of the sources familiar said Driscoll has been “aggressive” in getting buy-in from general officers to spearhead and deliver on these efforts, given his limited tenure. 

During his tenure, Driscoll, a former venture capitalist, formed a close working relationship with the former Army’s chief of staff, Gen. Randy George, who was ousted from his role in early April by Hegseth. 

President Trump and Hegseth then picked Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army vice chief of staff, to serve as the Army’s acting chief of staff. LaNeve, who is a former military aide to Hegseth, has met with senators in recent months, but his confirmation is in question over objections from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. 

The Army Secretary has also been involved in a simmering battle for influence with Hegseth, with tension flaring late last year when Trump picked Driscoll to negotiate with Ukrainian officials in hopes of ending the Russia-Ukraine war, The Hill previously reported. 

Last year, Driscoll and George, whose firing has drawn criticism from GOP lawmakers, rolled out the so-called Army Transformation Initiative last year, which was intended to focus on three areas: “deliver critical warfighting capabilities, optimize our force structure and eliminate waste and obsolete programs.” 

Among the fields of focus were integrating drones and artificial intelligence into Army formations, 

Driscoll’s expected departure was reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal. 

The Army is planning to phase out a unit that was studying and incorporating lessons from overseas wars, including the use of unmanned systems in the Russia-Ukraine war, The Hill reported on Thursday. 

The battalion, part of the 173rd Airborne Brigade, was backed by senior Army leadership, including George and Gen. Chris Donahue, the former commander of U.S. Army Europe and Africa.

data.title: President makes final push for Darline Graham in trip to 'Trump country'
data.description:
Myrtle Beach, S.C. — President Trump travelled south to rally support for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Friday ahead of next week’s primary runoff and urged Republicans to turn out in November’s midterm elections.

“I think Lindsey respected Darline more than any other person he knows including me, and that does not make me happy,” Trump quipped, referring to Graham’s late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died last month.

Graham joined Trump on stage at one point during rally, declaring “this is Trump country.” 

The president hit South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews without naming her, labeling her as “far left.

He did name Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, who are both locked in close races with Trump-backed GOP candidates.

The president also sought to use the rally to push Republican turnout in November. 

“We have to make the midterm elections too big to rig,” he said, alluding to his frequent and unfounded claims of election fraud.

The president acknowledged issues Republicans face in turning out their base when he is not at the top of the ballot. 

“What I want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” he said. 

Trump also warned supporters that Democrats will move to impeach him if Republicans lose their majorities in Congress. 

“I’m going to be impeached. They’re going to impeach me. They have no idea why,” he said. 

The president addressed non-campaign related issues as well.

He took the opportunity to celebrate the Supreme Court’s ruling on Friday that allowed construction on the White House ballroom to continue, at least until the appeal receives a full review.

“I’m in a very good mood tonight,” Trump said, referring to news of the ruling. 

Trump also declared that he views the Strait of Hormuz as a U.S. territory after saying last week he wanted to annex the waterway. Trump has shifted from military strikes to threats of economic isolation in his push to force concessions from Tehran.

The primary runoff marks a major test for Trump’s endorsement as Graham, a political newcomer temporarily appointed to her brother’s seat, runs to keep it for another six years. She is facing off against Rep. Ralph Norman, a real estate developer elected to the House in 2017.

Graham made headlines earlier this week at a televised debate with Norman when she flubbed a question on Taiwan and the South China Sea, saying national security was not her thing.

The answer was a sea change between her and her late brother, who was known as a foreign policy giant in the Senate. It was also met with immediate criticism from Norman and his allies.

Trump defended Graham’s response to the question ahead of his trip to South Carolina on Friday. 

“She’s very smart, and she was being honest. She’s into the price of groceries. … She is going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants,” Trump said before boarding Air Force One. 

“She understands that national security is my thing. … I thought it was a very honest answer,” he continued.

Graham enters the primary with an advantage from Trump’s endorsement and her status as Lindsey Graham’s sister. Trump won the state by nearly 18 points in 2024, by 11 points in 2020, and by 14 points in 2016. 

The winner of Tuesday’s runoff will run against Andrews. 

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the state’s Senate race as solid Republican, but nationally Republicans are facing headwinds amid Trump’s declining approval ratings and rising Democratic enthusiasm. 

Trump’s approval rating in South Carolina sits at 42 percent, according to a Civiqs tracking poll.

data.title: Teen drops high-profile social media addiction lawsuit
data.description:
A teenager has dropped her lawsuit against Meta, YouTube and Snapchat, which was set to go to trial later this year as part of a broader series of cases accusing social media giants of designing addictive platforms.

The teen, referred to as P.M.Y., previously settled with TikTok and “chose to dismiss the remainder so she could try to resume her life,” her attorney Emily Jeffcott said in a statement.

“PMY initiated this process with the goal of holding social media companies accountable and to push for changes to protect young people like herself,” Jeffcott said, adding, “She is ready to close this chapter and focus on moving forward.”

She had accused the companies of contributing to her social media addiction, depression and self-harm, according to Reuters.

Thousands of lawsuits against the companies have been consolidated into a single legal proceeding in Los Angeles Superior Court. Her lawsuit was scheduled to be heard by a jury in October as a bellwether trial, which are used as test cases for the broader litigation.

The first trial got underway in January. A jury ultimately found Meta and YouTube liable for negligently designing their platforms in March and ordered the companies to pay a combined $6 million. Both Snapchat and TikTok settled the case before trial.

R.K.C., the minor bringing another case set to go to trial, ultimately settled with Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube, and dropped his lawsuit against Meta last month.

“Another plaintiff in the personal injury trials has dropped her case against Meta after settling with TikTok,” Meta said in a statement after P.M.Y. opted to dismiss her lawsuit.

“This plaintiff had a significant mental health condition that pre-dated her use of social media, and it’s clear that many of these cases fit the same pattern,” the company added. “We’ll continue defending ourselves vigorously in court.”

Google spokesperson José Castaneda noted in a statement that P.M.Y. “voluntarily withdrew their claims against YouTube without payment.” Google is YouTube’s parent company.

He suggested this affirms the company’s “longstanding position that we provide safe, age-appropriate experiences and strong parental controls for young people and families.”

A spokesperson for Snap Inc., the owner of Snapchat, said in a statement that the company remains “focused on strengthening the safeguards, tools, and educational resources that support the safety, privacy, and well-being of all Snapchatters.”

data.title: White House rips Rosie O'Donnell for Trump, Harp jokes: She's 'a total slob'
data.description:
The White House responded Thursday to comments made by comedian Rosie O’Donnell while hosting “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” concerning President Trump and his administration.

Davis Ingle, a representative for the White House, said in a statement to news outlets that “Rosie O’Donnell is a nasty woman and a total slob whose brain has been completely destroyed by Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

O’Donnell hosted the program for three days where she made nods in her opening monologues to the president, referring to him as “orange Voldemort” in her final broadcast Thursday before performing a song.

“Poor Donny boy, your polls, your polls are falling. Your reflecting pool is green as Mountain Dew. Your wig’s a mess, your ballroom is appalling, and with Iran you bit off more than you can chew,” she sang.

She finished the song by calling for Trump to resign and “make this country great again.”

The jabs add to the contentious relationship O’Donnell and Trump have had in the past few years as O’Donnell moved to Ireland last year to escape the president’s second administration.

She has remained an open critic to Trump’s leadership style and agenda while the president has poked fun at her appearance and IQ.

“Because of the fact that Rosie O’Donnell is not in the best interests of our Great Country, I am giving serious consideration to taking away her Citizenship,” Trump wrote in a social media post last year.

O’Donnell also chimed into an ongoing conversation about the proximity between Trump and longtime White House aide Natalie Harp.

“It’s time to hang up your wig and let Natalie tuck you in,” she said during Wednesday’s show.

Harp has been in the center of media headlines since Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) slammed her during a campaign speech Sunday.

Several Trump administration officials have come to Harp’s defense, including the president’s son Eric Trump, who called Ossoff’s comments “absolute trash.”

data.title: Trump eyes vaccine categories
data.description:
Click in for more news from The Hill
{beacon}

Healthcare

Healthcare

 

The Big Story 

Trump eyes vaccine categories

To support President Trump’s vaccine executive order issued earlier this month, the administration is considering to changing or adding to the categories of vaccinations, in what critics argue is another effort by the White House to undermine existing vaccine policies. 

Jacquelyn Martin, Associated Press

A Request for Information (RFI) filed on Friday by the Department of Health and Human Service (HHS) asks for public comment on whether current federal categories for vaccinations are “adequate.” 

 

Vaccines are categorized as routine (universal), risk-based or shared clinical decision-making (SCDM).

 

“The Department seeks comment on these categories and whether additional or different categories should be adopted,” the RFI states. 

 

As the document notes, SCDM was adopted by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in 2019. SCDM applies to vaccines are those that a provider and patient can discuss and decide whether they would have benefits for that individual. 

 

In his executive order earlier this month, Trump called for moving certain childhood vaccines from being universal to being either risk-based or SCDM, reducing the number of routine immunizations from 18 to 11. 

 

Health care attorney Richard Hughes IV blasted the RFI in a memo Friday. 

 

“Whether or not the development of the SCDM category is considered beneficial, considerable ACIP deliberation went into its creation. Under the guise of simply requesting information, the administration is now making clear its intent to modify existing recommendation categories, or even create new ones,” wrote Hughes. 

 

“Perhaps even more troubling is what the RFI does not say. It makes no mention of ACIP, the body charged with developing vaccine recommendations since 1964, whose recommendations are the indispensable legal trigger for ACA coverage mandates, VFC program scope, EPSDT obligations, Medicare Part D zero-cost-sharing, and pharmacist scope-of-practice authority across dozens of states,” he added. 

 

The public can submit comments until September 20, 2026. 

 

Welcome to The Hill’s Healthcare newsletter, we’re Nathaniel Weixel and Joseph Choi — every week we follow the latest moves on how Washington impacts your health.

 

Did someone forward you this newsletter? Subscribe here.
